name: Gareth Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a CNC router at a family kitchen cabinet factory, loading board sheets and checking cutters before the panels go for edging. I have a vocational certificate and years on that table, and the wage is better than most operator jobs. I like knowing that a kitchen we cut may last twenty years, even if the dust bothers my chest.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who is at home, and what do you do outside the plant?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Claire works mornings in a primary-school office, and our school-age children Owen and Megan are fifteen and twelve. We have a mortgage, over a year saved and a small terraced rental house; plenty of other factories are nearby. I fit shelves for paying neighbours at weekends and use an AI chat tool now and then to check a rough price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the cabinet crew the office can keep its little AI shortcuts. A customer still wants a square kitchen panel and someone to fit the shelves properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our family factory pays me well for router work, and Claire’s school-office wage comes in regularly. The rented terrace and more than a year saved give us space to handle a slow month of weekend joinery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep loading the CNC router, checking cutters and taking booked Saturday shelf jobs. I would keep using the same AI chat tool now and then to price small jobs, and put part of each new paid fitting fee into savings after materials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel calm about work. The dust still gets in my chest, but I know the cuts and the people who order them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you check a price from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I compare it with the timber invoice and my hours before I quote anyone. The tool gives me a starting number, not the price I send.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the rental house bring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives us another source of income, though repairs and an empty month still happen. We do not spend next year’s rent before a tenant pays it.

I would leave **small AI shortcuts** to the office.
think: My **higher router wage** and Claire’s pay are steady.
A **year saved** and rental property can absorb a slow fitting month.
do: Keep **CNC router shifts** and check worn cutters.
Take **booked Saturday shelves** and use the existing chat tool for quotes.
Save part of **new fitting fees** after materials are paid.
feel: **Calm** about familiar factory work and household finances.

fieldNote: Gareth’s **existing chat use** supports occasional job pricing without new training.
His **strong cushion** includes savings and a rented house, while further savings require paid fitting work.

steps.text: Keep router shifts and take booked Saturday shelf jobs
Save new fitting fees left after materials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the owner that the factory must stay competitive, but trained router hands deserve first chance at any new loader jobs. I have seen other plants bring in loaders only after proper guards were fitted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordering software could change the office first, while a robot loader may later remove one of our two router places. Claire’s school wage and the rental property help, but losing my higher factory pay would still put a hole in our plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my router shift and ask for the next staffing rota. If the factory offers a paid, guarded loader practice place, I would take it after a qualified setter shows the stop procedure; if my hours fall, I would apply for posted reachable router jobs only at bill-covering pay and take more booked weekend fitting when customers actually call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about one of the router places going. A training video would not tell me where the moving sheet can catch a sleeve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI more on the side jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep using my existing chat tool for rough prices. I would only learn a new AI drawing checker if a client paid for a real design job and I could compare it against measured walls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a useful loader trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An actual paid slot behind a tested guard, with the machine stopped for the first changeover. If management only shows a video, I would ask again rather than claim I can run it.

The **factory wage** matters despite Claire’s pay and rental income.
do: Keep **current router shift** and request the staffing rota.
Take **paid guarded loader practice** only if an actual supervised slot is offered.
Apply after **hours fall** only for posted reachable bill-covering router work.

Take more paid fitting only when customers book after hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the village that thinking AGI might arrive in 2028, while robots able to load sheets and fit kitchens come around 2031. Our factory planning could change first, but the physical work has a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most router shifts to vanish once a machine can load and label every panel. The weekend fitting could also thin when robots work in houses; Claire’s pay, rent and savings help, but I would lie awake wondering whether they cover a long loss of my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cancel the planned new car and holiday, keep paid shifts while offered, and ask the owner for written staffing dates. If my hours end, I would apply only for posted reachable work at a wage covering our mortgage and bills; I would take paid fitting dates only when customers confirm them and ask the lender about temporary terms if no adequate role appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed about losing a large part of our income. I could keep working with timber, but I cannot make customers book me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you sell the rental house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not do that on a forecast. We would check its actual rent and repairs with the mortgage before deciding whether a sale helped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Owen about a trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my son Owen that his apprenticeship must lead to a real paid place, not just my memory of how safe joinery once felt. He gets to choose his work.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AI** from 2031 physical robots.
I would ask for **written staffing dates** before the router crew shrinks.
think: I expect **most router shifts** to go after capable robots arrive.
Rental and **cash savings** may not replace lost wages and fitting fees indefinitely.
do: Cancel **car and holiday** and keep offered paid shifts.
Apply after **lost hours** only for posted reachable bill-covering work.
Take **confirmed paid fitting** and ask lender about terms if no adequate job appears.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major income loss and broken sleep.
S2.quote: I could keep working with timber, but I cannot make customers book me.
fieldNote: His **thinking-AI risk** lies in planning before capable robots reach router loading and house fitting.
The **rental house** is not automatically sold; paid side work, new jobs and lender relief remain conditional.

steps.text: Cancel planned car and holiday and request written staffing dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the cabinet owner that thinking AGI in 2031 and capable fitting robots around 2034 leave a few years to keep customers loyal. I would rather earn a recommendation from a real kitchen than argue with a forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At forty-eight I will still need the mortgage paid, but I might have enough booked fittings to leave the router before robots arrive. A few Saturdays are not enough; I need reliable work through winter as well as summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my factory shifts and collect written prices and deposits for fitting jobs over the next year. If twelve months of confirmed fitting income after materials covers our household bills and we keep six months of expenses saved, I would leave the factory for full-time fitting; if that test fails, I would stay on the router and apply for posted nearby operator work only after hours actually fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, but the extra time lets me test the winter order book. A kitchen fitted in January tells me more than a summer queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the owner send you work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask, but I would count a fitting only when a customer signs and pays a deposit. A friendly promise from the office is not an order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a van now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would use my current vehicle until paid work covers a van as well as the mortgage, and I would get the insurance price first.

I would separate **2031 planning AI** from later physical robots.

Winter **fitting demand** must hold before I leave the factory.

feel: **Anxious**, with time to test real winter demand.

fieldNote: He tests **full-time fitting** against twelve months of actual income after materials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell neighbours that thinking AGI in 2036 and capable cabinet robots around 2039 leave time to build a customer book properly. A family firm should train its people while it still has paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be fifty-three when thinking systems arrive and fifty-six when robots may handle sheets and kitchens. Owen and Megan will be adults, but I cannot assume our mortgage, the tenant or my back will be trouble-free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the router shifts and put a fresh amount from each full wage month against the mortgage. If fitting jobs over several years produce twelve months of bill-covering income after materials and we retain six months saved, I would move into full-time fitting; in the first year after 2036 I would keep that business only while confirmed customers pay enough, or apply for posted reachable work if it fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about distant robots and calm enough to test fitting slowly. The rented terrace gives us room, but no tenant signs forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you wait for retirement instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the mortgage and pension numbers with Claire first. I cannot promise to stop work just because the calendar says I am older.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Owen and Megan the order book, including the empty weeks. I would tell them to ask about paid apprenticeships and choose work they can actually live on.

I would distinguish **2036 AI** from 2039 physical robots.

My **back and customer book** matter before I leave paid shifts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could take router shifts and make paid fitting uncertain before I have a full customer book. Written staffing dates, safe paid instruction and posted nearby jobs at bill-covering wages would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the cabinets that are still standing after twenty years. I know which cutter made the front of Mrs Pritchard’s kitchen, and that still matters to me.

headlineQuote: I like knowing that a kitchen we cut may last twenty years, even if the dust bothers my chest.
portrait: **Gareth**, 43, runs a cabinet router with a vocational certificate, strong factory pay and paid weekend shelf-fitting work.
His **school-office partner**, two school-age children, mortgage, year-plus savings and rental terrace give him several household buffers.
He uses **AI occasionally** for quotes and accepts proven machines only with offered paid guarded practice.
Fast robots threaten **router and fitting pay**; longer warning lets him test a full year of confirmed customers.
biggestWorry: **Fast physical robots** could remove router hours and weaken paid fitting demand around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, offered paid safe instruction and posted reachable bill-covering jobs would help.
